GORGO: Maximizing KV-Cache Reuse While Minimizing Network Latency in Cross-Region LLM Load Balancing

Alessio Ricci Toniolo Affiliation: Arcadia Research Team Correspondence to: alessio@arcadiaresearch.team    Abinaya Dinesh Affiliation: Arcadia Research Team    Rome Thorstenson Affiliation: Arcadia Research Team
Abstract

Distributing LLM inference across geographical regions can improve Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) by regionalizing service deployments. While existing multi-region load balancers save prefill computation by prioritizing Key--Value (KV) Cache hit rate, they ignore cluster networking latency, a critical factor in routing decisions. We introduce GORGO, a method for minimizing TTFT by optimizing a total serving cost as a function of available compute, network latency, and prefix caching. Using extensive profiling on custom infrastructure, we analyze component-level latency bottlenecks and benchmark GORGO against three baselines: (1) naive least-load routing, which ignores prefix-cache overlap; (2) prefix-similarity routing, which selectively pushes requests to the replica with the highest cached-prefix overlap; and (3) a centralized HTTP proxy that runs the GORGO policy while tracking requests across all nodes. We demonstrate that GORGO reduces P99 TTFT through network-aware routing and improves average TTFT by preventing pathological cross-region forwarding. Additionally, we find that GORGO-proxy overcomes synchronization overhead in previous methods and is 2.5x faster on median TTFT, demonstrating the success of a centralized router.11 1 Code is available at https://github.com/atoniolo76/gotoni/tree/benchmark-load-balancing. Note that AI tools were used in drafting, code writing, and editing of this paper (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026).

Keywords: 
Machine Learning

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) inference is increasingly deployed on geo-distributed GPU clusters, driven by the need to serve geographically distributed users while maintaining low latency and high availability. Recent multi-region systems have shown that routing across regions can also improve utilization by aggregating diurnally shifting demand (Xia et al., 2025). In this setting, however, requests have unpredictable output lengths and can take anywhere from milliseconds to minutes to complete, making load difficult to anticipate and coordinate. The dominant user-facing metric for interactive applications is often Time-to-First-Token (TTFT); a single misrouted request that incurs unnecessary wide-area latency or queuing can dominate tail performance (Dean and Barroso, 2013; Suresh et al., 2015), even if the system-level throughput remains high.

LLM inference can be decomposed into two computational phases: prefill and decode. Prefill processes the input prompt and constructs KV cache state, while decode generates output tokens autoregressively (Yu et al., 2022; Kwon et al., 2023). Prefix caching can reduce TTFT by reusing cached KV state from recurring system prompts, prior conversation turns, or other shared context (Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2024).

In a distributed deployment, each region hosts replicas with their own local KV caches. Routing requests toward a replica (or region) with higher prefix overlap can therefore reduce prefill work, but several factors complicate this decision: a target may be busy, unavailable, or queued, and cross-region forwarding incurs wide-area latency (Xia et al., 2025; Vulimiri et al., 2015). Load balancing policies must therefore model the tradeoff between KV-cache reuse, network, and queueing costs.

A central challenge is: when is it better to forward a request to a distant region with lower cache overlap versus serve it locally with higher cache hit rates? Existing approaches often prioritize cache overlap while treating network latency as a secondary or negligible concern. We demonstrate that network latency and KV cache similarity must be jointly optimized.

Our contribution: we introduce GORGO, a per-region load balancer that routes requests locally when possible, but selectively forwards to peer regions using a joint optimization over (i) prefix-cache locality, (ii) measured inter-region latency, and (iii) instantaneous admission/queue state. This is enabled by low-latency, low-bandwidth observability that continuously propagates peer network metrics to every deployed load balancer. We benchmark GORGO against three baselines: (1) naive least-load routing, (2) prefix-similarity routing that ignores network costs, and (3) a centralized HTTP proxy that tracks prefix-cache state and network latency to route requests.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first review existing multi-region and cache-aware routing strategies and motivate the network–cache tradeoff that GORGO targets. We then describe GORGO’s architecture and cost function before presenting an empirical evaluation.

2 Background and Motivation

2.1 Serving Primitives: Continuous Batching and KV Caching

Modern LLM serving stacks are built around two structural facts: (i) inference is stateful due to the Key–Value (KV) cache, and (ii) throughput depends on how well the system can admit new requests into a running batch. Orca introduced iteration-level scheduling (often referred to as continuous batching), in which requests are admitted and retired at each decoding iteration to improve GPU utilization and reduce padding waste (Yu et al., 2022). vLLM complements this by making KV-cache memory management explicit: PagedAttention stores KV blocks non-contiguously to reduce fragmentation and improve serving throughput (Kwon et al., 2023).

KV caching also enables prefix reuse: when multiple requests share an identical prefix (e.g., system prompts or shared conversation context), the serving system can reuse cached KV state to skip redundant prefill computation. SGLang’s RadixAttention operationalizes this mechanism using a radix-trie representation that supports automatic KV reuse across structured generation calls (Zheng et al., 2024).

2.2 Prefix-Aware Routing and Its Coordination Costs

Because the benefit of prefix reuse depends on where prior KV state resides, request placement becomes a routing problem. Preble demonstrates that prefix-aware scheduling can increase cache utilization by routing requests with shared prefixes to replicas likely to contain the corresponding KV cache state (Srivatsa et al., 2024). DLPM further explores distributed prompt management and scheduling, emphasizing that prefix-aware policies must balance locality with system-level objectives such as fairness and coordination overhead (Cao et al., 2025).

A central tension is that accurate prefix-aware routing typically requires tracking (or approximating) per-replica cache state. Centralized coordinators can maintain a global view, but their control-plane costs and tail latency penalties grow with cluster scale and KV-cache size (Cao et al., 2025).

2.3 Geo-Distributed Inference and Cross-Region Routing

Multi-region deployments are motivated by availability, latency to globally distributed users, and cost efficiency when demand shifts across regions over the day. SkyServe represents this broader trend toward multi-region serving frameworks that manage placement and operation across regions and clouds (Mao et al., 2025). Building on this setting, SkyWalker argues that cross-region traffic handling can exploit diurnal demand skew to provision closer to global peak, while mitigating the performance penalty of misrouting through a geo-distributed load-balancer architecture with KV-cache-aware routing and selective pushing (Xia et al., 2025).

A key systems constraint in geo-distributed routing is wide-area latency. Empirical characterizations of inter-region network behavior report typical intercontinental round-trip times on the order of tens to hundreds of milliseconds (Vulimiri et al., 2015). These costs interact directly with TTFT when a request is forwarded across regions.

In production, multi-cluster and cross-region gateways (e.g., GKE multi-cluster Gateways and AWS Bedrock cross-region inference) provide global routing and failover mechanisms. However, these interfaces largely treat inference as an opaque service endpoint, rather than incorporating LLM-specific signals such as KV-cache locality or continuous-batch admission capacity (Google Cloud, 2026; Amazon Web Services, 2026). In contrast, commercial systems such as Modal support prefix caching within a single region, but do not optimize routing across geographical deployments or account for cross-region latency (Modal, 2026b). In practice, regionalized deployments can also be constrained by market conditions (e.g., not all GPU types are available in all regions across all providers); systems such as SkyPilot address this by aggregating capacity across clouds (Yang and others, 2023).

2.4 Routing Objectives and the Network–Cache Tradeoff

Taken together, prior work establishes that KV-cache locality is a first-order determinant of serving efficiency (Xia et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2024; Srivatsa et al., 2024; Kwon et al., 2023), while geo-routing introduces non-trivial network costs (Vulimiri et al., 2015). Classical load balancing mechanisms such as consistent hashing provide stable request-to-backend mappings with minimal disruption under membership changes (Karger et al., 1997) (and related distributed lookup protocols such as Chord (Stoica et al., 2003)), and thus are frequently used as lightweight affinity mechanisms.

Nevertheless, affinity signals alone are insufficient for TTFT-sensitive workloads in geo-distributed clusters: maximizing prefix overlap can increase TTFT if the routing decision induces a large cross-region latency penalty or queues behind a saturated continuous batch.

For example, a request arriving at a West Coast load balancer finds the local region in a low-utilization state, providing a baseline for optimal performance. However, as regional traffic bursts, the balancer must choose between:

  • •

    US-West (High Load): 3 ms network latency, 5% cache hit, 6,500 running tokens (∼\sim300 ms delay) →⁣∼\rightarrow{}\sim303 ms TTFT, 305.59 ms total.

  • •

    Germany (Direct): 281 ms network latency, 0% cache hit, 0 running tokens →⁣∼\rightarrow{}\sim281 ms TTFT, 295.75 ms total.

  • •

    Israel (Queued): 183 ms network latency, 15% cache hit, 4,200 queued tokens (∼\sim195.75 ms delay) →⁣∼\rightarrow{}\sim378 ms TTFT, 378.75 ms total.

Existing policies either pick (1) by default or always pick (3) for maximum cache utilization. This motivates GORGO’s central question: how should a load balancer jointly account for (i) expected prefill savings from prefix reuse, (ii) measured network latency, and (iii) instantaneous queueing/admission state when selecting a serving region to minimize TTFT, particularly at the tail?

3 Routing and the GORGO Policy

3.1 Initial Geo-proximal Routing

Requests are initially sent to the proxy’s chat-completion endpoint for geo-proximal routing. We pre-hash messages from the WildChat dataset and utilize a Lookup Table of hashes to global coordinates. The haversine distance is calculated from the WildChat user’s coordinates to every node’s coordinates. Using the minimum calculated distance, a new request is constructed and sent to the respective load balancer endpoint.

3.2 Design objective and signal requirements

GORGO targets the network–cache tradeoff by selecting a serving region that minimizes estimated TTFT, jointly accounting for prefix reuse, network latency, and instantaneous load.

Concretely, a GORGO load balancer relies on three signals:

  1. 1.

    Cache locality: estimated prefill time between incoming requests and prefix overlap in each region.

  2. 2.

    Network latency: measured round-trip latency (RTT) between load balancers.

  3. 3.

    Admission/queue state: whether local regions can admit a new request promptly under continuous batching.

3.3 System architecture and routing workflow

GORGO uses a distributed, per-region load balancer architecture. Each region runs a loadbalancer.go instance that serves as client ingress, mirrors local serving state, and periodically exchanges summarized state with peer load balancers.

Local control state.

Each load balancer maintains a lightweight prefix index that mirrors the serving SGLang’s prefix structure, which represents cached prefixes using a radix trie (Zheng et al., 2024). The load balancer also mirrors local admission state (e.g., running vs. waiting requests) and maintains per-token timing statistics exported by the runtime.

Peer summaries.

Load balancers maintain a peer table with recent RTT measurements and refreshed summaries of peer availability and prefix-locality estimates.

Per-request decision.

For each region, the load balancer estimates TTFT as (a) forwarding latency, plus (b) residual prefill time after accounting for prefix reuse, plus (c) queueing/admission delay. Requests are forwarded only when the local region cannot immediately admit them into a running batch, and the request can optionally stay in the local region depending on the queue-size estimate.

3.4 Per-request objective: cost model

GORGO implements this decision using an additive cost model because components occur sequentially:

Cost⁡(region)\displaystyle\mathrm{Cost}(\text{region}) =NetworkLatency⁡(peer)\displaystyle=\mathrm{NetworkLatency}(\text{peer})
+tp⋅PrefillCost(peer + local)\displaystyle\quad+t_{\text{p}}\cdot\mathrm{PrefillCost}(\text{peer + local})
+q^s⋅QueueWaitTime(local).\displaystyle\quad+\hat{q}_{s}\cdot\mathrm{QueueWaitTime}(\text{local}).

Here, NetworkLatency⁡(peer)\mathrm{NetworkLatency}(\text{peer}) is the measured RTT to the peer load balancer; PrefillCost⁡(peer + local)\mathrm{PrefillCost}(\text{peer + local}) estimates the portion of prefill work not covered by prefix reuse using the measured per-token prefill rate; and QueueWaitTime⁡(peer)\mathrm{QueueWaitTime}(\text{peer}) estimates admission delay from mirrored requests in the queue and current running batch. The weights tpt_{\text{p}} and q^s\hat{q}_{s} are tunable at runtime.

Translating prefix overlap into time.

Given an estimated cached-prefix length LhitL_{\text{hit}} and total prefill length LpL_{\text{p}}, we convert overlap into time using the runtime’s per-token prefill time tpt_{\text{p}}:

SavedTime\displaystyle\mathrm{SavedTime} =Lhit⋅tp,\displaystyle=L_{\text{hit}}\cdot t_{\text{p}},
ResidualPrefillTime\displaystyle\mathrm{ResidualPrefillTime} =(Lp−Lhit)⋅tp.\displaystyle=(L_{\text{p}}-L_{\text{hit}})\cdot t_{\text{p}}.

3.5 Implementation

Telemetry and request tracing

The load balancer records per-request metadata needed to measure bottlenecks and to reconstruct routing paths:

  • •

    request creation timestamp and unique request identifier

  • •

    the sequence of load balancers traversed, with per-hop timestamps

  • •

    time from creation to admission by an executing region

Each load balancer also reports aggregate metrics (total requests handled, uptime/downtime intervals, and instantaneous queue depth).

Handler path.

Upon receiving a request, Handler() first pre-calculates the token count from the request body. If localHasCapacity() returns true (based on polled SGLang metrics: running requests below threshold and GPU cache below limit), the request is processed locally via reverse proxy.

When local capacity is exhausted and the hop count is below MaxHops, selectPeer() consults the configured strategy. All queued request lengths are multiplied by tpt_{p}.

Prefix index.

The prefix trie structure stores mappings from prompt prefixes to peer nodes that have previously served matching requests. During peer selection, the trie is traversed to find the longest matching prefix, enabling KV-cache-aware routing without storing actual KV pairs.

Serving-runtime integration (SGLang) and queue mirroring.

The serving runtime exposes a status endpoint that provides (i) current queue state, (ii) available KV-cache capacity, and (iii) per-token computation time. SGLang provides the radix-trie mechanism enabling prefix reuse (Zheng et al., 2024), and continuous batching motivates explicit admission/queue mirroring (Yu et al., 2022).

Central observability service.

For experiments and debugging, we also run a lightweight SGLang polling service that periodically pulls metrics from all load balancers to provide a consolidated view of state (including RTT measurements and NumWaitingRequests).

4 Experimental Evaluation

This section describes the experimental methodology used to evaluate GORGO. Our goal is to assess whether incorporating measured wide-area latency, prefix-cache locality, and admission/queue state into a single per-request decision improves user-visible latency, as measured by TTFT.

4.1 Setup

For these trials, we leverage three geographically distributed regions, each consisting of an 8xA100 node: West Coast (US), Germany (EU), and Israel (ME). Each instance in the region runs one GORGO load balancer and one SGLang inference server (§3), allowing it to make decisions leveraging regional and cross-regional compute. Models were provided by HuggingFace and held constant throughout experiments. All results here were recovered from inference requests on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3.

4.2 Parameter Tuning

In order to measure the tpt_{\text{p}} variable, we benchmark our SGLang server on 87 Wildchat dataset samples and measure the linear correlation between input tokens and TTFT 1.

4.3 Workload

Our work leverages GuideLLM, WildChat, and a geoproximal integration between the two to benchmark GORGO. This encompasses a synthetic mixed request distribution across regions with variable prompt lengths, including shared system prompts to induce non-trivial prefix overlap. In WildChat, requests follow multi-turn dialogue patterns similar to prior public traces (Zhao et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2023). In GuideLLM, we are able to vary workloads between four major types: concurrent, poisson, throughput, and sweep-based.

  1. 1.

    Concurrent workloads enable us to compute the maximal sustainable throughput of each load-balancing policy, as it maintains a fixed number of parallel requests in flight and consistently replaces completed requests.

  2. 2.

    Poisson workloads model human-like behavior by sending requests at a Poisson-distributed rate, mimicking bursty traffic patterns. Testing at a variable rate enables us to measure improvements at tail latencies (P99).

  3. 3.

    Throughput based request-firing enables us to zoom in on load balancing behavior when there are greater requests/second than what is available in the server running, available, and waiting queues.

  4. 4.

    Sweep-based workloads progressively increase request rate until latency degrades or errors appear.

Finally, we integrate WildChat with GuideLLM to benchmark our load balancing policies against simple geo-proximal routing. Since GuideLLM only supports targeting a single endpoint, we leverage the location metadata included in each WildChat conversation. First, we preprocess WildChat to create a lookup table mapping hash(prompt) → (lat, lon) and export prompts as a JSONL dataset. Then, we run a local geo-routing tunnel that GuideLLM targets. When the proxy receives a request, it hashes the prompt, looks up the user’s location, and forwards the request to the geographically nearest cluster node.

4.4 Baselines

We compare against four routing policies that represent common design points:

  1. 1.

    Least-load routing naively routes each request to the instance with the highest availability.

  2. 2.

    Prefix-similarity routing (Prefixtrie) routes to maximize cached-prefix overlap, without accounting for inter-cluster network latency and gpu availability.

  3. 3.

    GORGO accounts for local estimated TTFT (based on queue sizes), point to point latency, KV cache overlap to other peers, and GPU availability §3.

  4. 4.

    GORGO-proxy acts as a middleware node by serving a http-proxy that runs the GORGO policy with centralized information about incoming requests and instance-based metrics.

4.5 Results

On median TTFT (ms), GORGO-proxy (A. Table 5) achieves a 2.5x reduction in median TTFT (A. Table 2) compared to least-load, 2.5x faster than prefix-trie (A. Table 3), and 2.4x faster than GORGO. (A. Table 4). Figures 2 and 3 show the median and mean metrics, respectively, across methods.

4.6 Benchmark and Instrumentation

Each run lasts 60 seconds and processes requests from simulated users distributed globally, with 10 concurrent requests kept in flight at all times using GuideLLM. This sustained load allows us to effectively measure server behavior under pressure. We record per-request timestamps at each routing stage (load-balancer ingress/egress and inter-region forwarding) to compute TTFT with microsecond-resolution timestamps. Our benchmarking and measurement practices are informed by prior guidance on LLM serving benchmarking (Modal, 2026a).

5 Discussion

Interpreting the routing objective.

The motivating premise of GORGO is that minimizing TTFT in geo-distributed serving is fundamentally a multi-signal decision problem. Prefix reuse reduces prefill work, but the value of that reuse depends on the latency of the forwarding path and the likelihood of prompt admission under continuous batching (§3). Framing routing as the minimization of an estimated TTFT—rather than as “maximize cache overlap” or “minimize load” in isolation—makes the network–cache tradeoff explicit and highlights why policies optimized for throughput can be misaligned with TTFT-sensitive workloads.

Why an additive cost model is a useful abstraction.

GORGO’s cost model aggregates three terms that are already present in the serving pipeline: forwarding latency, residual prefill time after accounting for prefix reuse, and admission delay (§3). This decomposition clarifies which signals the load balancer must track (per-token compute rates, measured RTT, and admission/queue state) and provides a common interface for integrating cache-aware routing with geo-routing. Importantly, the model is not intended to perfectly predict per-request latency; rather, it operationalizes a consistent set of tradeoffs that can be evaluated and tuned within a deployment.

Centralized proxies versus coordination overhead.

Prior work in cross-regional inference has exclusively used distributed load balancers, assuming high overhead costs to synchronize a centralized load balancer (Xia et al., 2025). However, with GORGO-proxy, we show that a middleware proxy can achieve high throughput and an over 2x lower TTFT in highly distributed workloads, improving on the decentralized approach, GORGO. We find that by retaining the full-picture of every node’s KV-Cache and end-to-end latencies from proxy to node, the singular load balancer has a significant information advantage over individual load balancers. This is a direction for future work.

Design implications: avoiding pathological forwarding.

The explicit inclusion of network latency and admission state helps guard against pathological decisions in which a request is forwarded to chase cache overlap but incurs a larger latency penalty or queues behind an effectively saturated batch. From a systems perspective, this emphasizes that prefix locality is best treated as a means to reduce prefill cost, not as an end-to-end objective. It also suggests that cache-aware policies require a notion of “how much compute is actually saved” (via per-token rates) to be meaningfully compared against wide-area network costs and queueing risk.

Scope of applicability.

GORGO targets deployments where (i) requests are TTFT-sensitive, (ii) regions are connected by non-trivial wide-area latency, and (iii) the serving stack exposes admission state and stable per-token timing signals. Within this scope, GORGO’s architecture remains lightweight: it relies on summarized peer state and does not require centralized coordination or transfer of KV-cache contents.

Connection to prior systems.

Taken together, the discussion above motivates why GORGO should be interpreted as a bridge between cache-aware routing mechanisms and geo-distributed gateways: it adopts LLM-specific locality signals while making wide-area latency a first-class term in the routing decision. We next situate this design relative to prior systems in serving, prefix-aware placement, and geo-routing.

6 Related Work

Geo-distributed serving and inter-cloud orchestration.

A growing line of systems work studies how to provision and route services across regions and clouds to improve availability and cost efficiency. SkyServe and SkyWalker exemplify this trend for LLM inference, emphasizing geo-distributed deployments and the operational benefits of shifting capacity to follow diurnal demand (Mao et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2025). In parallel, general “sky computing” efforts such as SkyPilot focus on inter-cloud resource selection and job placement, abstracting away heterogeneity across providers while optimizing for performance/cost trade-offs (Yang and others, 2023). GORGO is complementary to these frameworks: rather than deciding where to run (or which cloud to use), our focus is the online request-routing decision once multiple regions are already deployed, and specifically on minimizing TTFT under LLM-specific statefulness.

LLM serving, KV caching, and prefix-aware routing.

Recent serving systems make the Key–Value (KV) cache a first-class concern and exploit prefix reuse to reduce redundant prefill computation. Single-region systems such as SGLang and vLLM operationalize prefix caching via explicit data structures and memory management, enabling reuse when many requests share common prompt prefixes (Zheng et al., 2024; Kwon et al., 2023). Preble extends this idea toward distributed settings by coordinating placement to increase prefix reuse and throughput (Srivatsa et al., 2024), and subsequent work explores more structured schedulers and fairness guarantees on top of prefix locality (e.g., DLPM) (Cao et al., 2025). These approaches motivate our use of prefix overlap as a routing signal, but they primarily target throughput and/or rely on centralized coordination. GORGO instead targets geo-distributed TTFT: we treat prefix locality as one input into a cost model that is explicitly co-optimized with wide-area latency and admission delay, and we do so in a per-region, distributed control plane.

Centralized vs. lightweight coordination for stateful routing.

A central scheduler can maintain a detailed global view of cache state and queue conditions, enabling high-quality placement decisions (Srivatsa et al., 2024; Cao et al., 2025). However, as deployments span regions, the control-plane RTT and the risk of a single failure domain become first-order concerns. GORGO occupies a different point in the design space: each region makes routing decisions locally using periodically exchanged summaries, aiming to preserve the benefits of cache-aware placement while avoiding tight, latency-sensitive coordination across regions.

Production multi-region gateways.

Commercial offerings expose cross-region inference and global endpoints—for instance, AWS Bedrock supports cross-region inference and GKE multi-cluster gateways provide a unified ingress across Kubernetes clusters (Amazon Web Services, 2026; Google Cloud, 2026). These systems provide robust failover and coarse traffic shifting, but largely treat inference as an opaque backend. In contrast, GORGO leverages LLM-specific signals (prefix locality and continuous-batching admission state) and makes network latency an explicit term in the routing objective, enabling decisions that directly target TTFT rather than only availability or aggregate load.

Managing prefill–decode imbalance and disaggregation.

As prompts become longer and more “prompt-heavy,” several systems address the prefill–decode imbalance using techniques such as chunked prefill and prefill/decode disaggregation across GPUs (Agrawal et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2024). Other work explores alternative reuse mechanisms (e.g., non-prefix sharing or kernel-level optimizations) that are largely orthogonal to routing (Liu and others, 2024; Xu and others, 2024). These advances reduce the compute component of TTFT, but do not by themselves resolve geo-routing trade-offs when cache locality and network latency conflict. GORGO is complementary: it assumes an underlying serving stack that may already use chunked prefill or disaggregation, and focuses on selecting the region where that stack should execute to minimize end-to-end TTFT.

Classic load balancing and scheduler designs.

Prior work on latency-sensitive datacenter scheduling often studies microsecond- scale tasks and emphasizes work stealing and fine-grained core reallocation (McClure et al., 2022; Ousterhout et al., 2019). These approaches inform our baselines and motivate treating admission and queueing explicitly, but their assumptions and coordination timescales differ from GPU-backed LLM inference (Yu et al., 2022).

7 Limitations

Trade-off between latency and throughput.

While GORGO excels in TTFT, the policy suffers with throughput (see Figures 2 and 3). In order to leverage selective pushing at scale and prevent queue overloading, we impose rate limits and queuing limits on individual instances. This may lead to GORGO overselecting for a TTFT-optimal route at the expense of underutilized compute. However, this problem is remediated by GORGO-proxy, which achieves both the lowest TTFT and greatest throughput by leveraging GORGO’s logical policy along with logs from inference backends for efficient hardware usage.

Methodological limitations.

Our routing decisions depend on the accuracy and freshness of four signals: measured RTT, estimated prefix overlap, mirrored admission/queue state, and per-token compute rates. In particular, prefix-overlap estimates are derived from a lightweight prefix index rather than from the serving runtime’s exact KV state, and per-token rates may shift with batch composition, prompt lengths, and system noise. These approximations can lead to misestimation of the true TTFT benefit of forwarding or cache reuse.

Experimental limitations.

The current evaluation is constrained to a small number of regions and a limited set of deployment configurations. However, three regions do capture the dominant intercontinental latency regimes while keeping experiments reproducible. We use WildChat as the primary data source driving our request mix, and treat it as representative of real-world usage. For posterity, we updated the GORGO policy to incorporate prompt-length characteristics from both the queue and currently running requests.

8 Future Work

Several directions follow naturally from these limitations.

On-device kernel for policy computation.

We find that the individual processes of tokenization and radix-trie traversal introduce non-zero latencies for GORGO. Prefixtrie, which neglects the calculation of the prefill time for a request, is computationally less-intensive due to fewer radix-trie searches and the lack of tokenization sidecar process. Future work could develop a native CUDA kernel for GPUs to perform the tokenization lookup and prefix trie search processes in parallel, dramatically speeding up the cost of calculation for efficient neural-network approaches (Jain et al., 2025).

Learning or adapting the cost weights.

The weights tpt_{p} and q^s\hat{q}_{s} are deployment parameters. Automatically tuning q^s\hat{q}_{s} using online feedback from observed TTFT and inter-token latency values could reduce manual calibration effort and improve robustness to changing network conditions and workload mixes. In general we deliberately focus on an interpretable, systems-driven policy to ensure predictability under changing network conditions, but learning-based routing is an avenue for future work.

Heterogeneous regions and policy constraints.

The current cost model assumes that per-token timing statistics are comparable within an experiment. Extending the model to heterogeneous accelerator fleets (e.g., different GPU types or memory capacities) would require normalizing compute-rate estimates and integrating capacity constraints. A related direction is to incorporate policy constraints (e.g., data residency) into the feasible set of routing targets.

Proactive prefix placement and cache warming.

GORGO is reactive: it routes based on current prefix locality and measured state. Proactively replicating or warming high-value prefixes in anticipation of demand shifts could reduce the need for cross-region forwarding while preserving cache reuse.

Robustness to GPU Failures and Slow Ranks

During development and evaluation of the GORGO policy, we found that GPU health was a major issue in high-throughput benchmark testing. In order to test our selective pushing GORGO-proxy, we ran maximum-throughput requests that would accumulate on the load balancer’s queue. This reached Linux’s file descriptor limit and required a system reboot, thus delaying our benchmarking process from completing. Modal, which operates a warm pool of over 20,000 GPUs, leverages a reliability dashboard for observing health metrics such as memory utilization and power usage (Belotti and Chang, 2025). We experimented with centralizing logging through running Grafana Alloy services and Prometheus visualization through polling SGLang’s ‘/metrics’ endpoint. Similarly, for training clusters with 100,000 GPUs, Meta developed a custom communication backend which pushes RDMA WQE events to a tracing database for identifying ‘Start’ to ‘Stop’ time discrepancies (Si et al., 2025). We developed our own tracing process with event-based pushing and circular buffering for profiling in Perfetto. Future work may improve the reliability of GPU clusters by adaptively responding to inference engine failures or sudden performance drops based on these methods.

9 Conclusion

Distributed LLM inference across geographical regions requires careful coordination between network topology and cache management. Existing approaches often optimize cache reuse and network latency independently, leading to either poor cache utilization (when routing ignores prefix locality) or degraded TTFT from cross-region forwarding (when routing ignores wide-area latency and queueing).

GORGO introduces a joint optimization framework that treats routing as a multi-objective problem, balancing network latency, KV cache similarity, and queue depths. By modeling routing cost as a function of all three factors, GORGO provides a principled approach to request placement that adapts to current network conditions and system load. While a heuristic policy and not a provably optimal scheduler, GORGO-proxy offers distinct advantages compared to existing solutions.

The key insight is that network latency and cache similarity should not be optimized independently. A high cache hit rate in a distant region may result in worse TTFT than a lower cache hit rate locally. GORGO’s cost function captures this trade-off explicitly, enabling intelligent routing decisions that minimize user-perceived latency.

As LLM deployments continue to scale globally, intelligent load balancing will become increasingly critical. GORGO provides a practical foundation for building responsive, efficient, and globally distributed LLM serving systems.

Impact Statement

This paper studies geo-distributed routing for LLM inference, with the goal of reducing Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and avoiding pathological cross-region forwarding. If deployed, such routing can improve responsiveness for globally distributed users and increase serving efficiency by better trading off network latency and KV-cache reuse. Improved efficiency may also reduce the energy and hardware required per request by avoiding redundant prefill computation.

From a systems perspective, cache-aware routing and telemetry introduce privacy and security considerations. While GORGO does not require moving KV-cache contents between regions, any practical deployment must ensure that routing metadata and measurements do not leak sensitive user information (e.g., through logs or timing side channels), and must respect policy constraints such as data residency. Mitigations include minimizing and anonymizing logged data, avoiding retention of raw prompts, enforcing strict access controls, and constraining the set of eligible regions according to regulatory and organizational policies.
